nameStory: The snowberry clearwing gets its name from its transparent wings that look like clear glass windows, and its caterpillars' favorite food: snowberry shrubs. The 'clearwing' part is obvious once you see one hovering at flowers—those see-through wings make it look almost magical in flight!
description: The snowberry clearwing is a day-flying moth that looks remarkably like a tiny hummingbird as it hovers at flowers. It has a fuzzy, reddish-brown body about the size of your thumb, with mostly transparent wings bordered in dark reddish-brown. These fascinating moths are often called 'hummingbird moths' because they feed on nectar just like hummingbirds, hovering in front of flowers with their long tongues extended.

idTips.label: Clear wings
idTips.description: Wings are mostly transparent like glass with dark reddish-brown borders, making a soft buzzing sound in flight that's quieter than a bee

idTips.label: Hovering behavior
idTips.description: Hovers motionless in front of flowers during daylight hours, wings beating so fast they're just a blur

idTips.label: Fuzzy body
idTips.description: Body is thick and fuzzy like a bumblebee's, colored reddish-brown to olive-brown, soft to touch if you could catch one

idTips.label: Long proboscis
idTips.description: Unfurls a long, thin tongue (proboscis) to reach deep into flowers, often extending it while still hovering

idTips.label: Yellow leg bands
idTips.description: Legs have distinctive yellow bands that flash as it moves from flower to flower

idTips.label: Daytime activity
idTips.description: Active during bright daylight hours, unlike most moths which come out at night

habitat: Look for snowberry clearwings in sunny gardens, meadows, and woodland edges throughout New England where flowering plants are abundant. They're especially common around areas with their host plants—snowberry, honeysuckle, and dogbane—but will visit any nectar-rich flowers. You'll often spot them in suburban gardens visiting bee balm, phlox, and butterfly bush.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring and can be seen visiting early blooming flowers like lilac and apple blossoms.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most abundant, actively feeding at garden flowers and mating. Look for them on hot, sunny days hovering at bee balm, phlox, and butterfly bush.
seasonality.fall: Second generation adults may appear in early fall, but activity decreases as flowers become scarce and temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Overwinters as pupae in the soil, completely absent from view during cold months.

funFact: These moths can beat their wings up to 80 times per second while hovering—faster than a hummingbird—and they actually lose their wing scales during their first flight, which is how their wings become transparent!
confusionNotes: Most often confused with actual hummingbirds due to their size and hovering behavior, but moths have antennae (hummingbirds don't) and fuzzy bodies rather than feathers. Remember: if it has antennae and a fuzzy body, it's the moth!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'hummingbird moths,' these are true moths in the sphinx moth family, not birds at all. The nickname 'flying lobster' comes from their reddish coloration and the way their antennae stick out like lobster antennae, though this name is less commonly used.
compareHints: The snowberry clearwing is very similar to its cousin the hummingbird clearwing, but has yellow bands on its legs while the hummingbird clearwing has black legs. The snowberry clearwing also tends to be slightly more reddish-brown in color compared to the hummingbird clearwing's more olive-brown tones.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The hummingbird clearwing differs from its close relative, the snowberry clearwing, by having light-colored legs and a solid-colored belly without black stripes.
